title: Texas Instruments Touch & Tell
subtitle: The toddler computer with no keyboard — you answer by pointing at the picture
why_scout_cares: The TI Touch & Tell (1981) is a speech-synthesis learning toy whose entire input is a fingertip on a picture. The child slides a printed panel onto a 'position sensitive keyboard' — a membrane touch pad — and the machine asks a random question; the child answers by pointing at the cow, the elephant, or the number four on the panel. It is a touch-to-answer interface for pre-literate children three years before the HP-150 touchscreen, and its seven overlay libraries included an E.T. pack. The museum has the keyboard-era Speak & Spell, the barcode-wand Magic Wand, and the voice-only Voyager — but nothing where the answer is given by touching the printed page. A clean, strange, and genuinely influential dead end of consumer touch input.

research.title: Texas Instruments Touch & Tell
research.overview: The Texas Instruments Touch & Tell is a speech-synthesis learning toy introduced in 1981, shortly after the Speak & Spell line. It has no screen and no alphanumeric keyboard. One of several printed picture panels is placed over a large flat 'position sensitive keyboard' — a membrane touch pad — and the toy asks a random question ('Where is the cow?') using its voice synthesizer; the child answers by pointing at the picture with a fingertip. Musical tones and sound effects reward correct answers.

deepDive.heading: Origins
deepDive.text: DATAMATH's calculator museum dates the introduction to 1981, rated by Texas Instruments for children aged 2 to 5. Inside, the toy is built around three integrated circuits: a CD8012 (a 4-bit TMS1100 microcontroller with 2KB ROM and 128×4 bits RAM), a TMC0280/CD2802 (the TMS5110A Voice Synthesis Processor from the Speak & Spell family), and a TMC0355/CD2601 Voice Synthesis Memory with 16K bits. The same housing and technology were reused for a medical aid, the Vocaid, which let mute people speak by pressing picture keys.

deepDive.heading: Interaction
deepDive.text: The interaction model is the point: the printed overlay IS the interface. The machine's question is randomized, the answer surface is the picture itself, and the child's body — a finger — is the pointer. Seven Touch & Tell Picture Panel Libraries were released at $17.95 each: Alphabet Fun, Animal Friends, All About Me, Number Fun, Little Creatures, World of Transportation, and an E.T. pack teaching character recognition and object identification from the film.

deepDive.heading: The family
deepDive.text: Texas Instruments shipped country-specific variants in the same housing — the UK Touch & Tell, France's Le Livre Magique, Germany's Tipp & Sprich, and Italy's Libro Parlante. The idea evolved into the more advanced Touch & Discover, and later the Super Speak & Read with two position-sensitive keyboards and the smaller Teddy Touch & Tell. The same 'answer by pointing' logic without any keyboard appears in the museum's TI Voyager.

deepDive.heading: Why it matters
deepDive.text: Touch & Tell is a consumer touch-input device for toddlers from 1981: direct manipulation of a picture by pointing, long before multitouch tablets made tap-the-answer the default interaction for preschool software. It belongs to the museum's TI speech-toy lineage (Speak & Spell, Magic Wand, Voyager, Little Professor) while being the only one whose input is pure pointing at a printed surface.
